$comment: Named benchmark sets: a fixed list of matches, so two revisions are measured on the same
thing. A round that says 'this won 4 of 5 on smoke against the control's 1 of 5' has made a
comparison; a round that says 'we lost again' on a random map, a random faction and a random
seed has made an anecdote, because faction, map and opponent all moved at once.
Seeds are arbitrary constants. Their only job is to be the same next time, so do not change
one to chase a nicer number - that silently invalidates every stored result for the set.
Add a new set instead. Factions are pinned for the same reason: consecutive rounds that
played GDI then Nod were comparing two different games.
A fixed list is also something a champion can be fitted to by repeated selection, which is
why the training loop's gate is hard-16-9-fresh: a set with a 'sequential' block instead of
matches, whose seeds are drawn fresh for every champion. See that set's own comment.

sets.name: smoke
sets.summary: Five matches, both factions, one map. The quickest thing that is still a measurement.

sets.name: standard
sets.summary: Two maps by both factions by three seeds. The set to quote in a round's result.

sets.name: hard-16-9
sets.summary: Eight pinned Hard matches on the training map, with two seeds for every faction matchup.

sets.name: hard-16-9-wide
sets.summary: Sixteen pinned Hard matches on the training map: four seeds for every faction matchup.
$comment: Seeds became worth multiplying once the engine stopped seeding the opponent AI from the
wall clock. Before that, every bot module drew from World.LocalRandom, which was
constructed with no seed, so a pinned lobby seed reproduced the map and nothing that the
opponent did - the same revision on seed 300002 scored anywhere from 0.108 to 1.000.
A seed now names a reproducible opponent, so a wider set buys scenario coverage rather
than repeat sampling of one noisy draw.
Every seed here has been played to completion. 310002 and 310008 were the first choices
and were replaced by 310012 and 310018: the first reproducibly hit the 2400-second
stalemate cap, the second crashed the battle process. A pinned seed that always fails
costs the same compute as one that answers something.

sets.name: hard-holdout
sets.summary: Eight pinned Hard matches on two maps the Hard training set never uses. Never train on this.
$comment: A promotion set is something a change can be fitted to: a deterministic benchmark is a
fixed list of games, and a change that only suits those games will pass it. This set
exists to be the thing that was not optimised against, so a promoted change can be asked
whether it generalised. Keep its maps and seeds disjoint from every other set, and do not
promote on it - read it.
Every match listed here has been run to completion on this harness. blue-mountains was
dropped after its Nod mirror failed the battle process twice on the same seed: a holdout
that cannot complete is worse than a smaller one, because a single failed match still
voids the whole sitting. Add maps by running them first, not by naming them.

sets.name: hard-16-9-fresh
sets.summary: The promotion gate: fresh Hard seeds on the training map for every champion, played in stages of 16 until a sequential test decides.
$comment: Eight pinned seeds stopped working as a gate once the champion had been selected on them.
By 27 September the champion won all eight, a candidate could at best tie, the fitness
tie-break caps at 1.0 in a win, and twenty rounds running promoted nothing - while the same
champion won only 4 of the 7 random-seed fights it provably played. Selecting repeatedly on
a small fixed set had fitted the champion to that set.
This set has no fixed matches. When a champion is first evaluated, the gate draws a pool
of maxPairs seeds it has never used before, starting at seedBase and never reusing one,
stratified so every stage holds each faction pairing equally. Candidates play the pool a
stage at a time; the champion's games on it are cached, because a seed replays exactly
(one cached game is replayed per evaluation to show it still does). A promotion retires
the pool, so no champion is ever judged on the seeds it was chosen on.
The verdict is Wald's sequential probability ratio test on the games only one arm won:
alpha is the rate at which a change that does nothing is promoted, beta the rate at which
one that wins discordantWinShare of those games is missed. Simulated against this bot's
measured behaviour (a 60% win rate, 30% of games decided differently), a neutral change is
promoted about 2% of the time and a 10-point-worse one never; a change worth +10 points
of win rate passes about 37% of the time, +15 points 72% and +20 points 95%, after 50 to
70 pairs on average. Smaller effects are invisible at this budget, and 'inconclusive' says
so rather than calling them failures. State lives in <runs>/<bot>/gate/<set>.json.
